cor-bauer-fike-normal.title: Bauer–Fike for Normal Matrices
cor-bauer-fike-normal.html:
1. Let A∈Mn(C) be normal with eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, and let E∈Mn(C). Then every eigenvalue μ of A+E satisfies mini|λi−μ|≤‖E‖2.
  2. Let A∈Mn(C) be diagonalizable. Then inf{κ2(X):X−1AX is diagonal}=1, the infimum over invertible X, if and only if A is normal.

cor-diagonally-dominant-invertible.title: Strict Diagonal Dominance Implies Invertibility
cor-diagonally-dominant-invertible.html: Let n≥1 and A∈Mn(C). Call A strictly diagonally dominant (by rows) if |aii|>ri(A)=∑j≠i|aij|for **every** i=1,…,n. A strictly diagonally dominant matrix is invertible. The same holds if A is strictly diagonally dominant by columns, that is, if A⊤ is strictly diagonally dominant.

cor-eigenvector-perturbation.title: Perturbation of a Single Eigenvector
cor-eigenvector-perturbation.html: Let A,A~=A+E∈Mn(C) be Hermitian, let λi(A) be a simple eigenvalue of A with unit eigenvector x, and put γ:=minj≠i |λi(A)−λj(A)|>0. If ‖E‖2<γ/2, then λi(A~) is a simple eigenvalue of A~, and every unit eigenvector x~ of A~ for it satisfies sin⁡θ(x,x~) ≤ ‖E‖2γ−‖E‖2 ≤ 2‖E‖2γ.

cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian.title: Hoffman–Wielandt for Hermitian Matrices
cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian.html: Let A,B∈Mn(C) be Hermitian. Then ∑i=1n(λi(A)−λi(B))2 ≤ ‖A−B‖F2.

cor-irreducibly-dominant-invertible.title: Irreducible Diagonal Dominance Implies Invertibility
cor-irreducibly-dominant-invertible.html: Let n≥1 and let A∈Mn(C) be irreducible, with |aii|≥ri(A)for every i,|aii|>ri(A)for **at least one** i. Then A is invertible.

cor-isolated-gershgorin-disc.title: An Isolated Disc Holds One Eigenvalue
cor-isolated-gershgorin-disc.title_html: An Isolated Disc Holds One Eigenvalue
cor-isolated-gershgorin-disc.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) with n≥2, and suppose Di(A) is disjoint from Dj(A) for every j≠i.

  1. Di(A) contains exactly one eigenvalue of A, and it is algebraically simple.
  2. If A is real, that eigenvalue is real, and it lies in the interval [aii−ri(A),aii+ri(A)].

cor-positive-sylvester.title: Sylvester Bound for Positive Matrices
cor-positive-sylvester.html: Let S∈Mm(C) and T∈Mn(C) be Hermitian with S⪰αIm and T⪰βIn, where α+β>0. Then for every C∈Mm×n(C) the equation SX+XT=C has exactly one solution, and it satisfies ‖X‖2≤‖C‖2α+β,‖X‖F≤‖C‖Fα+β.

def-eigenvalue-condition-number.title: Condition Number of a Simple Eigenvalue
def-eigenvalue-condition-number.title_html: Condition Number of a Simple Eigenvalue
def-eigenvalue-condition-number.html: Let A∈Mn(C) and let λ be a simple eigenvalue of A, with a right eigenvector x and a left eigenvector y, so y∗A=λy∗. The condition number of λ is κA(λ):=‖x‖‖y‖|y∗x|.

def-gershgorin-discs.title: Gershgorin Discs
def-gershgorin-discs.html: Let n≥1 and A=(aij)∈Mn(C). For i=1,…,n, the i-th Gershgorin radius of A is the real number ri(A):=∑j≠i|aij| ≥0, the sum over all j∈{1,…,n} other than i, and the i-th Gershgorin disc is the closed disc Di(A):={z∈C:|z−aii|≤ri(A)}. The discs Di(A⊤), whose radii ri(A⊤)=∑j≠i|aji| are taken from the columns of A, are the column discs.

def-numerical-range.title: Numerical Range
def-numerical-range.html: Let A∈Mn(C). The numerical range of A is the subset of C W(A):={x∗Ax:x∈Cn, ‖x‖=1}.

def-principal-angles.title: Principal Angles
def-principal-angles.html: Let U,W⊆Fn be subspaces with 1≤k=dim⁡U≤l=dim⁡W, and let QU∈Mn×k(F) and QW∈Mn×l(F) be orthonormal basis matrices of U and W. The principal angles between U and W are the k numbers 0≤θ1≤θ2≤⋯≤θk≤π2 determined by cos⁡θi=σi(QW∗QU)(i=1,…,k). We write Θ(U,W)=diag(θ1,…,θk) and sin⁡Θ(U,W)=diag(sin⁡θ1,…,sin⁡θk).

def-sep.title: Separation
def-sep.html: Let A∈Mm(C) and B∈Mn(C). The separation of A and B is sepF(A,B):=min{‖AX−XB‖F:X∈Mm×n(C), ‖X‖F=1}.

eq-commutator-bound.html: ‖A∗A−AA∗‖F≤2(κ2(X)−1)‖Λ‖F⋅(‖A‖F+‖Λ‖F).

eq-davis-kahan-identity.html: Λ~2X−XΛ1=Q~2∗EQ1,

eq-diagonal-norm.html: ‖diag(d1,…,dn)‖p=maxj|dj|(p=1,2,∞).

eq-dilation-frobenius.html: ‖H(M)‖F2=‖M‖F2+‖M∗‖F2=2‖M‖F2.

eq-hoffman-wielandt-weights.html: ‖A−B‖F2=∑i,j=1n|wij|2|λi−μj|2.

eq-polar-factor-identity.html: V∗(A−B)−(A−B)∗U=WP−P+QW−Q=Q(W−I)+(W−I)P.

eq-projection-difference-split.html: ‖Dx‖2=‖(I−PW)x1‖2+‖PWx2‖2.

eq-sqrt-sylvester.html: S(S−T)+(S−T)T=S2−ST+ST−T2=P−Q.

exm-bauer-fike-two-by-two.title: A large corner, separated eigenvalues
exm-bauer-fike-two-by-two.html: Let M>0, A=(1M02), and E=εe2e1⊤ with 0<ε≤1. Diagonalize A in two ways, compute κ2 of each eigenvector matrix, and compare the Bauer–Fike bound with the exact movement of the eigenvalues.

exm-bendixson.title: A rectangle beats the discs
exm-bendixson.html: Let A=(32−41). Show that every eigenvalue of A has positive real part, using @thm-bendixson, and check that the Gershgorin discs cannot show it. Compare with the eigenvalues.

exm-brauer-invertible.title: Ovals where discs fail
exm-brauer-invertible.html: Let A=(410041111). Show that the Gershgorin discs cannot prove A invertible, and that the ovals can.

exm-davis-kahan-small-gap.title: A tiny perturbation that turns the eigenvectors through 45°
exm-davis-kahan-small-gap.title_html: A tiny perturbation that turns the eigenvectors through 45°
exm-davis-kahan-small-gap.html: Let 0<η<1 and A=(1+η001−η),E=η(−1111). Compare the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of A and of A~=A+E, and compute ‖E‖2.

exm-davis-kahan-two-by-two.title: The theorem and the corollary, side by side
exm-davis-kahan-two-by-two.title_html: The theorem and the corollary, side by side
exm-davis-kahan-two-by-two.html: Let A=diag(2,0) and E=34(0110). Find the exact angle between the eigenvectors of A and of A~=A+E for the larger eigenvalue, and compare it with the bounds of @thm-davis-kahan-frobenius and @cor-eigenvector-perturbation.

exm-eigenvector-cluster.title: A stable plane with unstable lines inside it
exm-eigenvector-cluster.title_html: A stable plane with unstable lines inside it
exm-eigenvector-cluster.html: Let 0<η<1 and A=(1+η0001−η000−2),E=η(−110110000). Compare what happens to the eigenvectors for 1±η with what happens to the plane they span. Then bound the motion of that plane under any Hermitian perturbation E′ with ‖E′‖2=ε<3−η.

exm-gershgorin-isolate-real-eigenvalue.title: Isolating a real eigenvalue by scaling
exm-gershgorin-isolate-real-eigenvalue.title_html: Isolating a real eigenvalue by scaling
exm-gershgorin-isolate-real-eigenvalue.html: Let A=(73−10−1−3111). Show that A has exactly one eigenvalue λ with |λ−7|≤2, and that it is real.

exm-gershgorin-scaling.title: Separating a disc by scaling
exm-gershgorin-scaling.html: For A=(6251−1111−1) of @exm-gershgorin-three, the row disc D1(A)={|z−6|≤7} overlaps {|z+1|≤2}. Find a scaling D=diag(d,1,1) whose row discs split into two disjoint groups, and find the range of d that does it.

exm-gershgorin-three.title: Discs, eigenvectors, and where each eigenvalue sits
exm-gershgorin-three.title_html: Discs, eigenvectors, and where each eigenvalue sits
exm-gershgorin-three.html: Let A=(6251−1111−1). Describe the regions given by @thm-gershgorin (a) and (b). Then check that (7,1,1), (−1,1,1) and (1,1,−2) are eigenvectors, and locate each eigenvalue in the disc the theorem assigns to it.

exm-hoffman-wielandt-fails.title: Every pairing fails
exm-hoffman-wielandt-fails.html: Let A=(130−1),B=(131−1). Show that A and B are diagonalizable but not normal, and that the inequality of @thm-hoffman-wielandt fails for every pairing of their eigenvalues.

exm-hoffman-wielandt-two-by-two.title: A Hermitian and a diagonal matrix
exm-hoffman-wielandt-two-by-two.title_html: A Hermitian and a diagonal matrix
exm-hoffman-wielandt-two-by-two.html: Let A=(2112),B=(i002+i). Both are normal. Compute ‖A−B‖F2, the cost of both pairings of the eigenvalues, and the matrix S of the proof. Which pairings satisfy the conclusion of @thm-hoffman-wielandt?

exm-jordan-root-perturbation.title: The Jordan block meets Elsner’s bound
exm-jordan-root-perturbation.title_html: The Jordan block meets Elsner’s bound
exm-jordan-root-perturbation.html: Let n≥2 and 0<ε≤1, and put A=Jn(0) and B=Jn(0)+εene1⊤. Compare the movement of the eigenvalues with Elsner’s bound, and show that no bound of the form C(‖A‖2+‖B‖2)1−α‖A−B‖2α with α>1/n can hold for all A,B∈Mn(C).

exm-kato-temple-tridiagonal.title: Bracketing the top eigenvalue
exm-kato-temple-tridiagonal.html: Let A=(210121012),x=13(1,1,1). Estimate λ1(A) from x: compute μ and ε, the interval given by @thm-hermitian-residual-bound, and the interval given by @thm-kato-temple, using only information that can be read off A without computing its eigenvalues. Compare with the true value λ1(A)=2+2.

exm-mirsky-one-entry.title: Two matrices that differ in one entry
exm-mirsky-one-entry.title_html: Two matrices that differ in one entry
exm-mirsky-one-entry.html: Let A=(2112) and B=(2102). Compute the singular values of both, and compare the two sides of @thm-mirsky-frobenius with what @cor-singular-value-perturbation alone would give.

exm-numerical-range-jordan.title: The numerical range of a Jordan block
exm-numerical-range-jordan.title_html: The numerical range of a Jordan block
exm-numerical-range-jordan.html: Show that W(J2(0))={z∈C:|z|≤12}.

exm-ostrowski-graded.title: A tiny eigenvalue under a change of variables
exm-ostrowski-graded.title_html: A tiny eigenvalue under a change of variables
exm-ostrowski-graded.html: Let A=diag(1,10−6) and S=(10t1) with t=10−2, the change of variables that adds t times the first coordinate to the second. Compute SAS∗ and E=SAS∗−A. What do @cor-weyl-monotone and @thm-ostrowski-relative say about λ2(SAS∗), and what is its true value?

exm-polar-factors-nearby.title: The polar factors of two nearby matrices
exm-polar-factors-nearby.title_html: The polar factors of two nearby matrices
exm-polar-factors-nearby.html: Let A=(3045), whose polar decomposition @exm-polar-2x2 found to be U=15(2−112), |A|=5(2112), with σ(A)=(35,5). Let B=(3065). Find the polar decomposition of B, compute ‖U−V‖, and compare it with @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation.

exm-positive-sylvester-sharp.title: The Bound Can Be Attained
exm-positive-sylvester-sharp.html: Let S=(2112), T=(1) and C=(4−4). Solve SX+XT=C and compare with @cor-positive-sylvester.

exm-residual-certificate.title: An error bar from one product
exm-residual-certificate.title_html: An error bar from one product
exm-residual-certificate.html: Let A=(2113), x^=(1,2) and μ=72. Compute the residual, and say what interval @thm-residual-bound certifies around μ. Then compare it with the truth.

exm-second-difference-taussky.title: The second-difference matrix
exm-second-difference-taussky.html: Show that Kn is invertible for every n≥1, and that its eigenvalues lie in the open interval (0,4).

exm-sep-far-below-gap.title: Separation Far Below the Gap
exm-sep-far-below-gap.html: For a real number t≥0, let A=(1t01),B=(0). Compute sepF(A,B) and compare it with the distance between the spectra. Then, for t=99/10, solve AX−XB=C with C=e2 and compare the size of the solution with the guess ‖C‖F/min|λi−μj|.

exm-sep-normal-pair.title: A Normal Pair
exm-sep-normal-pair.html: Let A=(2112),B=(0−110). Compute sepF(A,B) in two ways: from @thm-sep-normal, and from the singular values of K.

exm-sorted-pairing-three.title: Three numbers, six pairings
exm-sorted-pairing-three.html: Let a=(4,2,1) and b=(3,0,−1), both decreasing. Compute ∑i(ai−bσ(i))2 for all six σ∈S3, and find the cheapest and the dearest.

exm-triangular-eigenvalue-condition.title: The condition numbers of a triangular 2 \times 2 matrix
exm-triangular-eigenvalue-condition.title_html: The condition numbers of a triangular 2×2 matrix
exm-triangular-eigenvalue-condition.html:
Let a,b,d∈C with a≠d, and A=(ab0d).

  1. Compute κA(a) and κA(d).
  2. For a=1, b=M>0, d=2, compare with the smallest value of κ2(X) over all diagonalizing X.
  3. For the same matrix and E=E21, compute λ′(0) for the eigenvalue 1 from @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative, and compare with the exact eigenvalues of A+tE for M=100 and t=10−4.

exm-two-planes-in-r4.title: Two Planes in Four Dimensions
exm-two-planes-in-r4.html: Let U=span(e1,e2)⊆R4 and W=span(a,b), where a=(3,4,4,3),b=(3,−4,4,−3). Find the principal angles, a pair of principal vectors for each, the sines from @thm-sines-of-principal-angles, and ‖PU−PW‖ in both norms. Then check the last two numbers directly.

exr-bauer-fike-a1.title: A1
exr-bauer-fike-a1.html:
1. State @thm-bauer-fike with all its hypotheses.
  2. True or false: the constant κ2(X) in @thm-bauer-fike is determined by A. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: for every A,E∈Mn(C), every eigenvalue of A+E lies within ‖E‖2 of an eigenvalue of A. Justify your answer.
  4. What does @cor-bauer-fike-normal (a) give when A is normal, and which example shows that its constant cannot be lowered?
  5. In @thm-bauer-fike-defective, what exponent appears for small ‖E‖2, and what decides it?

exr-bauer-fike-b1.title: B1: A Bauer–Fike region
exr-bauer-fike-b1.html:
Let A=(1203).

  1. Find an eigenvector matrix X with columns of length 1, and compute κ2(X).
  2. Hence find r such that every eigenvalue of A+E lies within r of 1 or of 3 whenever ‖E‖2≤0.01.
  3. Compute the eigenvalues of A+0.01e2e1⊤ exactly, and compare their movement with r.

exr-bauer-fike-b2.title: B2: A residual certificate
exr-bauer-fike-b2.html:
Let A=(2112), x^=(10,9) and μ=3.

  1. Compute the residual r=Ax^−μx^ and η=‖r‖2/‖x^‖2.
  2. Hence show that A has an eigenvalue in the interval [3−η,3+η], without computing the eigenvalues of A.

exr-bauer-fike-b3.title: B3: A defective bound
exr-bauer-fike-b3.html:
Let A=J2(3).

  1. Explain why @thm-bauer-fike does not apply to A.
  2. Use @thm-bauer-fike-defective to find r such that every eigenvalue of A+E lies within r of 3 whenever ‖E‖2≤10−4.
  3. Compute the eigenvalues of A+10−4e2e1⊤, and compare.

exr-bauer-fike-c1.title: C1: One eigenvalue in each disc
exr-bauer-fike-c1.title_html: C1: One eigenvalue in each disc
exr-bauer-fike-c1.html:
Let A=XΛX−1 have n distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, put g=mini≠j|λi−λj|, and let E satisfy r=κ2(X)‖E‖2<g/2.

  1. Prove that for each i, A+E has exactly one eigenvalue in the disc {z:|z−λi|≤r}, and that A+E is diagonalizable.
  2. Deduce that if A and E are real and every λi is real, then every eigenvalue of A+E is real.

Hint: apply @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant to the path A+tE.

exr-bauer-fike-c2.title: C2: The best shift for a residual
exr-bauer-fike-c2.title_html: C2: The best shift for a residual
exr-bauer-fike-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and x^∈Cn with x^≠0, and put ρ=x^∗Ax^/x^∗x^.

  1. Prove that ‖Ax^−μx^‖2≥‖Ax^−ρx^‖2 for every μ∈C, with equality only for μ=ρ.
  2. Deduce that if A is normal, then A has an eigenvalue λ with |λ−ρ|≤‖Ax^−μx^‖2/‖x^‖2 for every μ∈C.

exr-continuity-of-roots-a1.title: A1
exr-continuity-of-roots-a1.html:
1. State @thm-roots-continuous, including both hypotheses on q.
  2. Which imported fact of analysis does the proof of @thm-roots-continuous use, and at which step? Which one does @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant use?
  3. True or false: if ‖B−A‖2≤10−8, then every eigenvalue of B lies within 10−8 of an eigenvalue of A. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A∈M3(C) and D1(A)∪D2(A) is disjoint from D3(A), then D1(A) contains exactly one eigenvalue. Justify your answer.
  5. What is the difference between the conclusions of @thm-elsner-spectral-variation and @thm-elsner-matching?

exr-continuity-of-roots-b1.title: B1: Cauchy’s bound
exr-continuity-of-roots-b1.html:
Let p(x)=x3−3x2+4x−12.

  1. Use @lem-cauchy-root-bound to bound the moduli of the roots of p.
  2. Find the roots exactly, and compare.

exr-continuity-of-roots-b2.title: B2: Counting with discs
exr-continuity-of-roots-b2.html:
Let A=(101−11220−21).

  1. Show that A has exactly one eigenvalue λ1 with |λ1−10|≤2, and that it is real.
  2. Explain why the Gershgorin discs cannot decide whether the other two eigenvalues are real.
  3. Use the trace to locate the sum of the other two eigenvalues in an interval.

exr-continuity-of-roots-c1.title: C1: Stability is an open condition
exr-continuity-of-roots-c1.title_html: C1: Stability is an open condition
exr-continuity-of-roots-c1.html:
1. Let p be monic of degree n with every root in the open disc {|z|<1}. Prove that there is δ>0 such that every monic q of degree n whose coefficients are within δ of those of p also has every root in {|z|<1}.
  2. Deduce that the set of A∈Mn(C) with ρ(A)<1 is open: for each such A there is η>0 with ρ(B)<1 whenever ‖B−A‖2<η.

exr-continuity-of-roots-c2.title: C2: Why one-sided bounds do not give a matching
exr-continuity-of-roots-c2.title_html: C2: Why one-sided bounds do not give a matching
exr-continuity-of-roots-c2.html:
For lists (λ1,…,λn) and (μ1,…,μn) of complex numbers and r≥0, say that the list of μ’s is r-close to the list of λ’s if every μj is within r of some λi.

  1. Let n=2. Prove that if each list is r-close to the other, then the μj can be numbered so that |λi−μi|≤r for i=1,2.
  2. Show that (a) fails for n=3: give two lists of length 3, each 0-close to the other, such that every numbering has maxi|λi−μi|=2.
  3. Explain why the proof of @thm-elsner-matching needs @lem-eigenvalue-count-constant, and cannot simply apply @thm-elsner-spectral-variation twice, once in each direction.

exr-continuity-of-roots-c3.title: C3: Sharpening Cauchy’s bound by rescaling
exr-continuity-of-roots-c3.title_html: C3: Sharpening Cauchy’s bound by rescaling
exr-continuity-of-roots-c3.html:
Let n≥1, let p(x)=xn+cn−1xn−1+⋯+c1x+c0∈C[x] be monic, and let s>0.

  1. Prove that q(y):=p(sy)/sn is monic of degree n, with coefficients cj/sn−j, and that z is a root of p if and only if z/s is a root of q. Hence deduce that every root z of p satisfies |z|≤s(1+max0≤j≤n−1|cj|sn−j).
  2. Apply (a) with s=3 to p(x)=x3−3x2+4x−12, and compare the bound with the one @lem-cauchy-root-bound gives directly and with the roots found in @exr-continuity-of-roots-b1.

exr-davis-kahan-a1.title: A1
exr-davis-kahan-a1.html:
1. State the subspace perturbation equation @eq-davis-kahan-identity, and say which matrix in it measures the principal angles.
  2. In @thm-davis-kahan-frobenius, which two lists of eigenvalues must be separated by δ? Why not the eigenvalues of A inside and outside the subspace?
  3. True or false: “if ‖E‖2 is tiny compared with ‖A‖2, then every unit eigenvector of A+E is close to a unit eigenvector of A”. Justify.
  4. Why is ‖sin⁡Θ‖2≤‖sin⁡Θ‖F, and when does @thm-davis-kahan-one-sided improve on what the Frobenius theorem gives for ‖sin⁡Θ‖2?
  5. Which earlier result turns the bound on the matrix X=Q~2∗Q1 into a bound on angles?

exr-davis-kahan-b1.title: B1: How far does the top eigenvector move?
exr-davis-kahan-b1.title_html: B1: How far does the top eigenvector move?
exr-davis-kahan-b1.html:
Let A=(50002000−1),E=12(010101010), and let x~ be a unit eigenvector of A~=A+E for its largest eigenvalue.

  1. Compute ‖E‖2 and the gap γ of λ1(A)=5.
  2. Use @cor-eigenvector-perturbation to bound sin⁡θ(e1,x~).
  3. Use @thm-davis-kahan-frobenius, with the separation estimated by @cor-weyl-perturbation, to obtain a better bound. Hence show that the angle is less than 13∘.
  4. Check that 2 is an eigenvalue of A~ and find the other two. Recompute the bound of (c) with the exact separation.

exr-davis-kahan-b2.title: B2: Which theorem applies?
exr-davis-kahan-b2.html:
In each case A and A~ are Hermitian 4×4 matrices, k=2, Λ1 lists the eigenvalues of A belonging to Q1, Λ~2 lists the eigenvalues of A~ belonging to Q~2, and ‖EQ1‖2=0.2, ‖EQ1‖F=0.25. Determine which of @thm-davis-kahan-frobenius and @thm-davis-kahan-one-sided apply, and give the best bound on sin⁡θk that they yield. Justify your answer.

  1. Λ1=diag(3,2), Λ~2=diag(0.4,−1).
  2. Λ1=diag(3,0), Λ~2=diag(1.9,5).
  3. Λ1=diag(2,1), Λ~2=diag(2,−1).
  4. Λ1=diag(−1,−2), Λ~2=diag(0.5,4).

exr-davis-kahan-b3.title: B3: The same bounds for the projections
exr-davis-kahan-b3.title_html: B3: The same bounds for the projections
exr-davis-kahan-b3.html: In the setting of @thm-davis-kahan-frobenius, let U=col(Q1) and W=col(Q~1), with orthogonal projections PU and PW. Prove that ‖PU−PW‖F≤2‖EQ1‖Fδ, and that under the hypotheses of @thm-davis-kahan-one-sided, ‖PU−PW‖2≤‖EQ1‖2/δ.

exr-davis-kahan-c1.title: C1: A bound that needs only the perturbed matrix
exr-davis-kahan-c1.title_html: C1: A bound that needs only the perturbed matrix
exr-davis-kahan-c1.html:
Let A~∈Mn(C) be Hermitian with Q~=(Q~1Q~2) and Λ~2 as in the text. Let Z∈Mn×k(C) be any matrix with orthonormal columns, not necessarily eigenvectors of anything, and put M=Z∗A~Z∈Mk(C),R=A~Z−ZM.

  1. Prove that if every eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix M differs from every diagonal entry of Λ~2 by at least δ>0, then the principal angles between col(Z) and col(Q~1) satisfy ‖sin⁡Θ‖F≤‖R‖F/δ.
  2. Deduce: let λi(A~) be a simple eigenvalue of A~, let z be a unit vector, μ=z∗A~z and r=A~z−μz. If every eigenvalue of A~ other than λi(A~) lies at distance at least δ from μ, then a unit eigenvector x~ for λi(A~) satisfies sin⁡θ(z,x~)≤‖r‖/δ.

Hint: diagonalize M and compute Q~2∗R in two ways.

exr-davis-kahan-c2.title: C2: The constant in the eigenvector bound is sharp
exr-davis-kahan-c2.title_html: C2: The constant in the eigenvector bound is sharp
exr-davis-kahan-c2.html:
Let g>0 and e>0, and let A=diag(g,0), E=e(0110).

  1. Show that a unit eigenvector x~ of A+E for its larger eigenvalue makes an angle θ∈[0,π/4) with e1 satisfying tan⁡2θ=2e/g.
  2. Deduce that sin⁡θ⋅g/e→1 as e→0+.
  3. Hence show that for no constant c<1 is it true that sin⁡θ(x,x~)≤c‖E‖2/γ for all sufficiently small Hermitian E, in the setting of @cor-eigenvector-perturbation.

exr-eigenvalue-condition-a1.title: A1
exr-eigenvalue-condition-a1.html:
1. Define the condition number κA(λ), saying for which λ it is defined.
  2. State the formula for the derivative of a simple eigenvalue of A+tE at t=0.
  3. True or false: for every eigenvalue of every A∈Mn(C), a right eigenvector x and a left eigenvector y satisfy y∗x≠0. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A=XΛX−1 with κ2(X)≥106, then some eigenvalue of A has κA(λ)≥106. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: κ2A+3I(2λ+3)=κA(λ) for every simple eigenvalue λ of A. Justify your answer.
  6. The proof of @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative needed eigenvectors of A+tE that converge as t→0. Where did they come from?

exr-eigenvalue-condition-b1.title: B1: Three condition numbers
exr-eigenvalue-condition-b1.html:
Let A=(130054002).

  1. For each eigenvalue of A, find a right and a left eigenvector with integer entries, and compute κA(1), κA(2) and κA(5).
  2. Hence decide which eigenvalue is the most sensitive to first order, and find E with ‖E‖2=1 for which that eigenvalue of A+tE has |λ′(0)| as large as possible.

exr-eigenvalue-condition-b2.title: B2: A derivative checked against the exact answer
exr-eigenvalue-condition-b2.title_html: B2: A derivative checked against the exact answer
exr-eigenvalue-condition-b2.html:
Let A=(01−23) and E=E12.

  1. Find the eigenvalues of A with right and left eigenvectors, and compute both condition numbers.
  2. Use @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative to find λ′(0) for each eigenvalue of A+tE.
  3. Find the eigenvalues of A+tE exactly. Hence compare the first-order estimate with the exact value at t=10−3.

exr-eigenvalue-condition-b3.title: B3: Invariance of the condition number
exr-eigenvalue-condition-b3.title_html: B3: Invariance of the condition number
exr-eigenvalue-condition-b3.html:
Let λ be a simple eigenvalue of A∈Mn(C). Prove that:

  1. λ― is a simple eigenvalue of A∗, and κA∗(λ―)=κA(λ);
  2. κU∗AU(λ)=κA(λ) for every unitary U.
  3. Explain why (b) fails for a general invertible S in place of U, using A=diag(1,2).

exr-eigenvalue-condition-c1.title: C1: Perfect conditioning characterizes normality
exr-eigenvalue-condition-c1.html:
1. Let A∈Mn(C) have n distinct eigenvalues. Prove that A is normal if and only if κA(λ)=1 for every eigenvalue λ.
  2. Show that the hypothesis of distinct eigenvalues cannot be replaced by “κA(λ)=1 for every simple eigenvalue λ”: give a non-normal A∈M3(C) with a simple eigenvalue, all of whose simple eigenvalues have condition number 1.

Hint: in (a), what does κ=1 say about y, and what does the computation in @thm-left-right-biorthogonal say about yj∗xi?

exr-eigenvalue-condition-c2.title: C2: The derivatives add up to the trace
exr-eigenvalue-condition-c2.title_html: C2: The derivatives add up to the trace
exr-eigenvalue-condition-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) have n distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, and let E∈Mn(C). Write λi(t) for the eigenvalue of A+tE near λi, from @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative.

  1. Prove that λ1′(0)+⋯+λn′(0)=trE.
  2. Deduce this again from tr(A+tE)=λ1(t)+⋯+λn(t), valid for all small t, and explain why the two arguments agree.

Hint: in (a), use a diagonalizing X and the rows of X−1 as left eigenvectors.

exr-eigenvalue-condition-c3.title: C3: The adjugate at a simple eigenvalue
exr-eigenvalue-condition-c3.title_html: C3: The adjugate at a simple eigenvalue
exr-eigenvalue-condition-c3.html:
Let n≥2, let λ be a simple eigenvalue of A∈Mn(C) with right eigenvector x and left eigenvector y, and put N=λI−A.

  1. Prove that adjN=cxy∗ for some scalar c≠0.
  2. Prove that tr(adjN)=pA′(λ), the derivative of the characteristic polynomial at λ.
  3. Deduce a second proof that y∗x≠0, and the formula adj(λI−A)=pA′(λ)xy∗y∗x.

Hint: for (a), use both products in @thm-adjugate-identity; for (b), apply @thm-derivative-of-det to t↦(λ+t)I−A.

exr-gershgorin-a1.title: A1
exr-gershgorin-a1.html:
1. Define the Gershgorin radius ri(A) and the disc Di(A), and state @thm-gershgorin, including the statement about the peak coordinate of an eigenvector.
  2. True or false: every Gershgorin disc of A contains an eigenvalue of A. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: every eigenvalue of A lies in ⋃i(Di(A)∩Di(A⊤)). Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: an invertible matrix is strictly diagonally dominant by rows or by columns. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: an irreducible matrix with |aii|≥ri(A) for every i is invertible. Justify your answer.
  6. Name the method of proof of @thm-gershgorin in one line.

exr-gershgorin-b1.title: B1: Deciding invertibility
exr-gershgorin-b1.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are invertible. Justify your answers, using the results of this section where they apply and a direct computation where they do not.

  1. (52−21−42034i)
  2. (312131113)
  3. (211121112)
  4. (110110012)

exr-gershgorin-b2.title: B2: An interval for a symmetric matrix
exr-gershgorin-b2.title_html: B2: An interval for a symmetric matrix
exr-gershgorin-b2.html:
Let A=(51−1131−116).

  1. Use @thm-gershgorin to find an interval containing every eigenvalue of A, and compare it with the interval [−‖A‖∞,‖A‖∞] given by @cor-spectral-radius-row-column-bound.
  2. Hence show that A is positive definite, and that detA lies between 1 and 83.

exr-gershgorin-b3.title: B3: Choosing the scaling
exr-gershgorin-b3.html:
Let A=(74410−1−1−2−1).

  1. Show that the row disc D1(A) meets the other two row discs.
  2. For D=diag(d,1,1) with d>0, find the scaled radii, and find all d for which the first scaled disc is disjoint from the other two.
  3. Check that (−6,−1,1) is an eigenvector of A, and that its eigenvalue lies in the first scaled disc for d=3.

exr-gershgorin-c1.title: C1: Dominance and definiteness
exr-gershgorin-c1.html:
1. Prove that a Hermitian matrix A with aii>ri(A) for every i is positive definite.
  2. Prove that a Hermitian irreducible matrix with aii≥ri(A) for every i, strictly for at least one i, is positive definite.
  3. Deduce that for every n≥1 and every real t≥0, the matrix Kn+te1e1⊤ is positive definite.

Hint for (b): apply (a)’s argument to find where the eigenvalues can be, and then use @thm-taussky.

exr-gershgorin-c2.title: C2: Irreducibility cannot be dropped
exr-gershgorin-c2.html:
1. Give a 3×3 reducible matrix with |aii|≥ri(A) for every i, strictly in at least one row, that is singular. Which step of the proof of @thm-taussky fails for it?
  2. Let A be irreducible and let λ be an eigenvalue with |λ−aii|≥ri(A) for every i. Prove that the eigenspace Eλ(A) has dimension 1.

Hint for (b): given two independent eigenvectors, form a combination with a zero coordinate.

exr-hermitian-perturbations-a1.title: A1
exr-hermitian-perturbations-a1.html:
1. State the Kato–Temple theorem, with its hypotheses.
  2. True or false: for Hermitian A, a unit vector x and real μ, the eigenvalue of A closest to μ is within ‖Ax−μx‖ of μ. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: for Hermitian A and invertible S, λk(SAS∗) and λk(A) have the same sign for every k. Justify your answer.
  4. Which of the three bounds of this section need information that is not contained in A, x and μ? What information?
  5. Why can the constant 1 in @cor-weyl-perturbation not be lowered, and why does that not contradict Ostrowski’s theorem?

exr-hermitian-perturbations-b1.title: B1: Three bounds for one estimate
exr-hermitian-perturbations-b1.title_html: B1: Three bounds for one estimate
exr-hermitian-perturbations-b1.html:
Let A=(5222) and x=110(3,1).

  1. Compute μ=x∗Ax and ε=‖Ax−μx‖, and the interval given by @thm-hermitian-residual-bound.
  2. Using @thm-cauchy-interlacing to bound λ2(A), apply @thm-kato-temple to bracket λ1(A).
  3. Find the eigenvalues of A exactly. Hence compare the actual error of μ with ε and with the Kato–Temple bound.

exr-hermitian-perturbations-b2.title: B2: Ostrowski’s factors
exr-hermitian-perturbations-b2.html: Let A=diag(2,−1) and S=(1101). Compute SAS∗ and its eigenvalues, the eigenvalues of SS∗, and the factors θ1,θ2 of @thm-ostrowski-relative. Hence verify the theorem for this pair.

exr-hermitian-perturbations-b3.title: B3: The Rayleigh quotient minimizes the residual
exr-hermitian-perturbations-b3.title_html: B3: The Rayleigh quotient minimizes the residual
exr-hermitian-perturbations-b3.html: Let A be Hermitian and x a unit vector, with ρ=x∗Ax. Prove that for every real ν, ‖Ax−νx‖2=‖Ax−ρx‖2+(ν−ρ)2. Hence deduce that among all real ν, the residual bound of @thm-hermitian-residual-bound is sharpest at ν=ρ.

exr-hermitian-perturbations-c1.title: C1: A residual that guarantees an eigenvalue
exr-hermitian-perturbations-c1.title_html: C1: A residual that guarantees an eigenvalue
exr-hermitian-perturbations-c1.html:
Let A be Hermitian, x a unit vector, μ=x∗Ax and ε=‖Ax−μx‖.

  1. Let α<μ<β. Prove that if ε2<(μ−α)(β−μ), then A has an eigenvalue in (α,β).
  2. Deduce that A has an eigenvalue in [μ−ε,μ+ε], which is @thm-hermitian-residual-bound again, for this choice of μ.

Hint for (a): if there is none, consider x∗(A−αI)(A−βI)x.

exr-hermitian-perturbations-c2.title: C2: Relative bounds need structured perturbations
exr-hermitian-perturbations-c2.title_html: C2: Relative bounds need structured perturbations
exr-hermitian-perturbations-c2.html:
1. Let A be Hermitian and S=I+F with F∈Mn(C). Prove that |λk(SAS∗)−λk(A)| ≤ (2‖F‖2+‖F‖22)|λk(A)| for every k, whenever S is invertible.
  2. Show that there is no constant c such that |λk(A+E)−λk(A)|≤c‖E‖2|λk(A)| for all Hermitian A, E and all k.

Hint for (a): expand SS∗−I, and show first that ‖F∗‖2=‖F‖2.

exr-hermitian-perturbations-c3.title: C3: Kato–Temple is sharp
exr-hermitian-perturbations-c3.html:
Let λ1>λ2 be real, A=diag(λ1,λ2), and x=(cos⁡ϕ,sin⁡ϕ) with 0<ϕ<π/2.

  1. Compute μ=x∗Ax and show that ε2=(λ1−λ2)2cos2⁡ϕsin2⁡ϕ.
  2. Show that @thm-kato-temple (b), with λ=λ1 and α=λ2, holds with equality. Hence the constant in the Kato–Temple bound cannot be improved.

exr-hoffman-wielandt-a1.title: A1
exr-hoffman-wielandt-a1.html:
1. State the Hoffman–Wielandt theorem, with its hypotheses.
  2. True or false: if A and B are normal, the eigenvalues of B listed in any order satisfy ∑i|λi−μi|2≤‖A−B‖F2. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality holds for every pair of diagonalizable matrices. Justify your answer.
  4. For normal A and B, what bound does the theorem give on the distance between an eigenvalue of B and its partner?
  5. Where exactly does Birkhoff’s theorem (@thm-birkhoff) enter the proof, and what would be missing without it?
  6. For Hermitian A, B with E=A−B of rank one, explain why at most one eigenvalue can move by the full amount ‖E‖2.

exr-hoffman-wielandt-b1.title: B1: A pair of normal matrices
exr-hoffman-wielandt-b1.title_html: B1: A pair of normal matrices
exr-hoffman-wielandt-b1.html: Let A=(0220),B=(100−1+2i). Check that both are normal, compute ‖A−B‖F2 and the costs of both pairings of the eigenvalues, and compute the matrix S of the proof of @thm-hoffman-wielandt. Hence decide which pairings satisfy the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality.

exr-hoffman-wielandt-b2.title: B2: Hermitian, compared with Weyl
exr-hoffman-wielandt-b2.html: Let A=(200010000),B=(21012000−1). Compute 𝛌λ(A), 𝛌λ(B), ‖A−B‖F and ‖A−B‖2. Verify @cor-hoffman-wielandt-hermitian and @cor-weyl-perturbation for this pair. Hence say which of the two bounds is closer to the truth here.

exr-hoffman-wielandt-b3.title: B3: Sorting
exr-hoffman-wielandt-b3.html: Let a=(5,2,−1) and b=(4,3,0). Compute ∑i(ai−bσ(i))2 for all six σ∈S3. Hence confirm @lem-sorted-pairing, and say which pairing is the most expensive.

exr-hoffman-wielandt-c1.title: C1: The most expensive pairing
exr-hoffman-wielandt-c1.html:
1. Let A,B∈Mn(C) be normal, with eigenvalues λi and μi. Prove that there is also a permutation σ with ∑i|λi−μσ(i)|2≥‖A−B‖F2.
  2. Deduce that for Hermitian A,B, ∑i=1n(λi(A)−λn+1−i(B))2 ≥ ‖A−B‖F2.

Hint for (b): apply @lem-sorted-pairing to the list −λn+1−i(B).

exr-hoffman-wielandt-c2.title: C2: Each eigenvalue keeps its own disc
exr-hoffman-wielandt-c2.title_html: C2: Each eigenvalue keeps its own disc
exr-hoffman-wielandt-c2.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be normal with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, and let δ=mini≠j|λi−λj|. Let B be normal with ‖A−B‖F<δ/2. Prove that each open disc {z:|z−λi|<δ/2} contains exactly one eigenvalue of B, counted with multiplicity. Explain why @cor-bauer-fike-normal alone does not give this.

exr-hoffman-wielandt-c3.title: C3: A Jordan block of any size
exr-hoffman-wielandt-c3.title_html: C3: A Jordan block of any size
exr-hoffman-wielandt-c3.html:
Let n≥2, ε>0, A=Jn(0) and B=Jn(0)+εEn1, where En1 is the matrix unit.

  1. Show that the characteristic polynomial of B is xn−ε, and hence that every pairing of the eigenvalues of A and B costs nε2/n.
  2. Deduce that the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality fails for every pairing whenever 0<ε<nn/(2n−2), and that the ratio of the cost to ‖A−B‖F2 tends to ∞ as ε→0+.

Hint for (a): expand det(xI−B) along the first column.

exr-inclusion-regions-a1.title: A1
exr-inclusion-regions-a1.html:
1. Define the Brauer oval Oij(A) and the numerical range W(A), and state the Toeplitz–Hausdorff theorem.
  2. True or false: W(A)=convspec(A) for every A∈Mn(C). Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: W(A) is contained in the union of the Gershgorin discs of A. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if A+A∗≻0, then A is invertible. Justify your answer.
  5. Why does @thm-brauer-ovals require n≥2?

exr-inclusion-regions-b1.title: B1: Invertibility from ovals
exr-inclusion-regions-b1.html:
Let A=(511151222).

  1. Show that neither the row discs nor the column discs of A exclude 0.
  2. Use @thm-brauer-ovals to show that A is invertible.
  3. Check that (1,−1,0) is an eigenvector, and verify that its eigenvalue lies in O12(A).

exr-inclusion-regions-b2.title: B2: A Bendixson rectangle
exr-inclusion-regions-b2.html: Let A=(13−11). Find the rectangle of @thm-bendixson, and hence show that every eigenvalue of A satisfies 0≤Reλ≤2 and |Imλ|≤2. Compare with the eigenvalues.

exr-inclusion-regions-b3.title: B3: Computing numerical ranges
exr-inclusion-regions-b3.html:
Determine W(A) for each matrix. Justify your answers.

  1. A=(1201)
  2. A=diag(1,i,−1,−i)
  3. A=(2112)

exr-inclusion-regions-c1.title: C1: Direct sums
exr-inclusion-regions-c1.html:
1. Let B∈Mk(C) and C∈Mm(C). Prove that W(B⊕C)=conv(W(B)∪W(C)).
  2. Deduce that A=diag(2,−2,2i,−2i)⊕J2(0) is not normal, but satisfies W(A)=convspec(A).

Hint for (a): one inclusion needs @thm-toeplitz-hausdorff.

exr-inclusion-regions-c2.title: C2: When the numerical range is real, or a point
exr-inclusion-regions-c2.title_html: C2: When the numerical range is real, or a point
exr-inclusion-regions-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C).

  1. Prove that W(A)⊆R if and only if A is Hermitian.
  2. Deduce that W(A)={c} for a single c∈C if and only if A=cI.

exr-inclusion-regions-c3.title: C3: The numerical radius
exr-inclusion-regions-c3.html:
For A∈Mn(C), the numerical radius is w(A)=max{|z|:z∈W(A)}.

  1. Explain why the maximum exists, and prove that ρ(A)≤w(A)≤‖A‖2.
  2. Prove that ‖A‖2≤2w(A).
  3. Show that both constants are attained: w(A)=‖A‖2 for every normal A, and ‖A‖2=2w(A) for A=J2(0).

Hint for (b): bound ‖H‖2 and ‖K‖2 separately.

exr-principal-angles-a1.title: A1
exr-principal-angles-a1.html:
1. Define the principal angles between subspaces U,W⊆Fn with 1≤dim⁡U≤dim⁡W.
  2. True or false: if U⊆W, then every principal angle between U and W is 0. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: the principal angle between span(u) and span(−u), for u≠0, is π. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if U∩W≠{0}, then θ1=0. Justify your answer.
  5. State the formula for ‖PU−PW‖2 in terms of principal angles, with its hypothesis.
  6. True or false: for two distinct lines U,W in R2, ‖PU−PW‖2<1. Justify your answer.

exr-principal-angles-b1.title: B1: Two planes in three dimensions
exr-principal-angles-b1.title_html: B1: Two planes in three dimensions
exr-principal-angles-b1.html:
Let U=span(e1,e2) and W=span((1,0,0),(1,3,4)) in R3.

  1. Find an orthonormal basis matrix of W.
  2. Compute the principal angles between U and W.
  3. Hence compute ‖PU−PW‖2 and ‖PU−PW‖F.
  4. Explain why θ1=0 could have been predicted without computation.

exr-principal-angles-b2.title: B2: Which projections are at distance one?
exr-principal-angles-b2.title_html: B2: Which projections are at distance one?
exr-principal-angles-b2.html:
Determine, for each pair, whether ‖PU−PW‖2=1. Justify your answer.

  1. U=span(e1,e2) and W=span(e2,e3) in R3.
  2. U=span((1,1,0)) and W=span((1,−1,1)) in R3.
  3. U=span(e1,e2) and W=span((1,0,1),(0,1,1)) in R3.
  4. U=span((1,2,3)) and W=span((1,0,0),(0,1,0)) in R3.

exr-principal-angles-b3.title: B3: Two lines
exr-principal-angles-b3.html: Let u,w∈Fn be unit vectors and c=|⟨u,w⟩|. Prove that ‖uu∗−ww∗‖2=1−c2,‖uu∗−ww∗‖F=21−c2.

exr-principal-angles-c1.title: C1: Counting zero and right angles
exr-principal-angles-c1.title_html: C1: Counting zero and right angles
exr-principal-angles-c1.html:
Let U,W⊆Fn with 1≤k=dim⁡U≤l=dim⁡W, orthonormal basis matrices QU,QW, and M=QW∗QU.

  1. Prove that y∗(Ik−M∗M)y=‖(I−PW)QUy‖2 for every y∈Fk.
  2. Deduce that the number of principal angles equal to 0 is dim⁡(U∩W).
  3. Prove that the number of principal angles equal to π/2 is dim⁡(U∩W⊥).

Hint for (b): a positive semidefinite matrix B with y∗By=0 has By=0.

exr-principal-angles-c2.title: C2: The smallest angle as a maximum
exr-principal-angles-c2.title_html: C2: The smallest angle as a maximum
exr-principal-angles-c2.html:
Let U,W⊆Fn with 1≤k=dim⁡U≤l=dim⁡W and principal angles θ1≤⋯≤θk.

  1. Prove that cos⁡θ1=max{|⟨u,w⟩|:u∈U, w∈W, ‖u‖=‖w‖=1}, and that the maximum is attained at the principal vectors u1,w1.
  2. Deduce that θ1 is the smallest principal angle between a line of U and a line of W, which is the notion tried and rejected at the start of the section.
  3. Hence explain, in one sentence, why θ1 alone cannot distinguish the pairs (U,W1) and (U,U) of the opening, but the full list θ1,θ2 can.

exr-singular-values-and-polar-a1.title: A1
exr-singular-values-and-polar-a1.html:
1. State Mirsky’s theorem. In its proof by the Hermitian dilation of @prp-hermitian-dilation, where does each of the two factors of 2 come from?
  2. True or false: |σi(A)−σi(B)|≤‖A−B‖F for every i. Justify.
  3. True or false: the unitary polar factor is a continuous function of A on the invertible matrices, and it extends continuously to all of Mn(C). Justify.
  4. Which identity turns the perturbation of a square root into a Sylvester equation, and which result then bounds it?
  5. Why does @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation hold in both the spectral and the Frobenius norm?

exr-singular-values-and-polar-b1.title: B1: Mirsky by hand
exr-singular-values-and-polar-b1.html:
Let A=(3045), with σ(A)=(35,5) from @exm-polar-2x2, and B=(3043).

  1. Show that σ(B)=(13+2,13−2).
  2. Verify @thm-mirsky-frobenius for this pair.
  3. What bound on ∑i(σi(A)−σi(B))2 does @cor-singular-value-perturbation give? Hence say what Mirsky’s theorem gains here.

exr-singular-values-and-polar-b2.title: B2: A square root that does not commute
exr-singular-values-and-polar-b2.title_html: B2: A square root that does not commute
exr-singular-values-and-polar-b2.html:
Let S=(3223), T=(3224), P=S2 and Q=T2.

  1. Compute P and Q, and explain why S=P1/2 and T=Q1/2.
  2. Find λ2(P) and λ2(Q)1/2.
  3. Compute ‖P−Q‖2 and ‖P−Q‖F, and hence the two bounds of @thm-sqrt-perturbation. Compare them with ‖S−T‖.

exr-singular-values-and-polar-b3.title: B3: A nearly sharp instance
exr-singular-values-and-polar-b3.html:
Let A=2I2 and B=(2−112).

  1. Find the polar decompositions of A and B.
  2. Compute ‖U−V‖2 and ‖U−V‖F, and compare them with the bounds of @thm-polar-unitary-perturbation.
  3. Compute ‖|A|−|B|‖2 and the bound of @thm-polar-positive-perturbation.

exr-singular-values-and-polar-c1.title: C1: The square root is continuous everywhere
exr-singular-values-and-polar-c1.title_html: C1: The square root is continuous everywhere
exr-singular-values-and-polar-c1.html:
Let S,T∈Mn(C) be positive semidefinite.

  1. Let λ be an eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix S−T, with unit eigenvector x. Prove that S2−T2=(S−T)2+(S−T)T+T(S−T), and that x∗(S2−T2)x=λ2+2λx∗Tx.
  2. Deduce that if λ≥0 then λ2≤‖S2−T2‖2.
  3. Prove that ‖P1/2−Q1/2‖2≤‖P−Q‖21/2 for all positive semidefinite P,Q∈Mn(C), and show that the exponent 12 cannot be replaced by anything larger.

Hint: for (c), apply (b) to the pair (S,T) or to the pair (T,S), according to the sign of the eigenvalue of S−T of largest modulus.

exr-singular-values-and-polar-c2.title: C2: Both Eckart–Young lower bounds from perturbation theory
exr-singular-values-and-polar-c2.title_html: C2: Both Eckart–Young lower bounds from perturbation theory
exr-singular-values-and-polar-c2.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(C), let 0≤k<p=min(m,n), and let B∈Mm×n(C) have rank at most k.

  1. Explain why σi(B)=0 for i>k.
  2. Prove, using @thm-mirsky-frobenius, that ‖A−B‖F2≥∑i=k+1pσi(A)2.
  3. Prove, using @cor-singular-value-perturbation, that ‖A−B‖2≥σk+1(A).
  4. Compare with @thm-eckart-young and @thm-eckart-young-spectral.

exr-singular-values-and-polar-c3.title: C3: The nearest unitary to an almost-unitary matrix
exr-singular-values-and-polar-c3.title_html: C3: The nearest unitary to an almost-unitary matrix
exr-singular-values-and-polar-c3.html:
Let E∈Mn(C) with ‖E‖2<1, let A=I+E, and let U be the unitary polar factor of A.

  1. Prove that σn(A)≥1−‖E‖2>0, so that A is invertible.
  2. Prove that ‖U−I‖≤2‖E‖/(2−‖E‖2) in both the spectral and the Frobenius norm.
  3. Deduce that if ‖E‖2≤12 then ‖U−I‖F≤43‖E‖F. Compare with the bound ‖U−I‖F≤2‖E‖F that @cor-unitary-nearest and the triangle inequality give with no computation.

exr-sylvester-bounds-a1.title: A1
exr-sylvester-bounds-a1.html:
1. Define sepF(A,B) for A∈Mm(C) and B∈Mn(C), and state how it is computed from the Kronecker matrix K.
  2. True or false: sepF(A,B)=mini,j|λi−μj| for all square A,B. Justify your answer.
  3. True or false: sepF(A+cIm,B+cIn)=sepF(A,B) for every c∈C. Justify your answer.
  4. State the bound on the solution of AX−XB=C in terms of the separation, including its hypothesis.
  5. In the proof of @thm-sylvester-one-sided, which vectors are the equation multiplied by, and where are the hypotheses A⪰αIm and B⪯βIn used?

exr-sylvester-bounds-b1.title: B1: A positive Sylvester equation
exr-sylvester-bounds-b1.html:
Let S=(3113),T=(1002),C=(34−3−4).

  1. Find the largest α and β with S⪰αI2 and T⪰βI2, and state the bound that @cor-positive-sylvester gives for ‖X‖2.
  2. Solve SX+XT=C, column by column.
  3. Compute ‖X‖2 and ‖C‖2, and check the bound. Hence decide whether the bound is attained here.

exr-sylvester-bounds-b2.title: B2: Separations of four pairs
exr-sylvester-bounds-b2.html:
For each pair, compute sepF(A,B) and decide whether it equals mini,j|λi−μj|. Justify your answer.

  1. A=diag(1,3), B=(0110).
  2. A=(2112), B=(−1).
  3. A=(0−220), B=diag(1,−1).
  4. A=(1401), B=(0).

exr-sylvester-bounds-b3.title: B3: A symmetric Sylvester equation
exr-sylvester-bounds-b3.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian with A⪰2In, and let C∈Mn(C).

  1. Prove that AX+XA=C has exactly one solution, and that it satisfies ‖X‖2≤‖C‖2/4.
  2. Prove that if C is Hermitian, then so is X.

exr-sylvester-bounds-c1.title: C1: The separation is stable, and it measures a distance
exr-sylvester-bounds-c1.title_html: C1: The separation is stable, and it measures a distance
exr-sylvester-bounds-c1.html:
Let A∈Mm(C), B∈Mn(C), E∈Mm(C) and F∈Mn(C).

  1. Prove that ‖EX‖F≤‖E‖2‖X‖F and ‖XF‖F≤‖F‖2‖X‖F for every X∈Mm×n(C).
  2. Prove that |sepF(A+E,B+F)−sepF(A,B)|≤‖E‖2+‖F‖2.
  3. Now let n=1 and B=(μ). Prove that there is E with ‖E‖2=sepF(A,B) such that μ is an eigenvalue of A+E.
  4. Hence, for t=99/10 in @exm-sep-far-below-gap, exhibit the size of a perturbation of A that makes 0 an eigenvalue, and explain why the eigenvalue gap 1 is a poor guide to how close the pair is to having a common eigenvalue.

Hint for (c): use a singular value decomposition of A−μIm.

exr-sylvester-bounds-c2.title: C2: Interlaced spectra break the spectral-norm bound
exr-sylvester-bounds-c2.title_html: C2: Interlaced spectra break the spectral-norm bound
exr-sylvester-bounds-c2.html:
Let A=diag(0,2), B=diag(1,3) and C=(111−1).

  1. Show that every eigenvalue of A is at distance at least 1 from every eigenvalue of B, and explain why @thm-sylvester-one-sided does not apply with α−β=1.
  2. Solve AX−XB=C.
  3. Show that ‖X‖2>‖C‖2.
  4. Verify directly that ‖X‖F≤‖C‖F, as @thm-sep-normal requires.

Hint for (c): compute C⊤C, and test X on the vector (1,1).

lem-cauchy-root-bound.title: Cauchy’s Bound for the Roots
lem-cauchy-root-bound.html: Let n≥1 and let p(x)=xn+cn−1xn−1+⋯+c1x+c0∈C[x] be monic. Put M=max0≤j≤n−1|cj|. Then every root z∈C of p satisfies |z|≤1+M.

lem-davis-kahan-identity.title: The Subspace Perturbation Equation
lem-davis-kahan-identity.html: In the notation above, Λ~2X−XΛ1=Q~2∗EQ1,{#eq-davis-kahan-identity} and the non-zero singular values of X are the non-zero sines sin⁡θi of the principal angles between U=col(Q1) and W=col(Q~1), with multiplicity. In particular ‖X‖F=‖sin⁡Θ(U,W)‖F,‖X‖2=sin⁡θk=‖sin⁡Θ(U,W)‖2, where sin⁡Θ(U,W)=diag(sin⁡θ1,…,sin⁡θk).

lem-doubly-stochastic-linear-min.title: A Fractional Pairing Is Never Cheaper
lem-doubly-stochastic-linear-min.title_html: A Fractional Pairing Is Never Cheaper
lem-doubly-stochastic-linear-min.html: Let C=(cij)∈Mn(R) and S=(sij)∈Ωn. Then there is a permutation σ∈Sn with ∑j=1ncσ(j)j ≤ ∑i,j=1nsijcij.

lem-eigenvalue-count-constant.title: Eigenvalue Counts Are Constant Along a Path
lem-eigenvalue-count-constant.title_html: Eigenvalue Counts Are Constant Along a Path
lem-eigenvalue-count-constant.html: Let A0,A1∈Mn(C), and put A(t)=(1−t)A0+tA1 for t∈[0,1]. Let K,L⊆C be sets at positive distance: there is d>0 with |z−w|≥d for all z∈K and w∈L. Suppose that for every t∈[0,1], every eigenvalue of A(t) lies in K∪L. Then the number N(t) of eigenvalues of A(t) in K, counted with algebraic multiplicity, does not depend on t. In particular N(0)=N(1).

lem-hermitian-parts.title: Real and Imaginary Parts of a Matrix
lem-hermitian-parts.title_html: Real and Imaginary Parts of a Matrix
lem-hermitian-parts.html: Let A∈Mn(C), and put H=A+A∗2,K=A−A∗2i. Then H and K are Hermitian, A=H+iK, and for every x∈Cn the numbers x∗Hx and x∗Kx are real, with Re(x∗Ax)=x∗Hx,Im(x∗Ax)=x∗Kx.

lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix.title: Orthonormal Basis Matrices
lem-orthonormal-basis-matrix.html:
Let U⊆Fn have dimension k≥1 and let Q∈Mn×k(F) be an orthonormal basis matrix of U.

  1. Q∗Q=Ik and PU=QQ∗.
  2. ‖Qy‖=‖y‖ for every y∈Fk. For every matrix Y with k rows and every matrix Z with k columns, ‖QY‖2=‖Y‖2,‖QY‖F=‖Y‖F,‖ZQ∗‖2=‖Z‖2,‖ZQ∗‖F=‖Z‖F.
  3. Every orthonormal basis matrix of U is QR for some R∈U(k) (orthogonal when F=R).
  4. In−PU=PU⊥. If moreover k<n and Q⊥∈Mn×(n−k)(F) is an orthonormal basis matrix of U⊥, then the square matrix (Q∣Q⊥) is unitary, and QQ∗+Q⊥Q⊥∗=In.

lem-perturbed-eigenvalue-resolvent.title: A Perturbed Eigenvalue Forces a Large Resolvent
lem-perturbed-eigenvalue-resolvent.title_html: A Perturbed Eigenvalue Forces a Large Resolvent
lem-perturbed-eigenvalue-resolvent.html: Let A,E∈Mn(C), let ‖⋅‖ be an operator norm on Mn(C) (@def-operator-norm), and let μ be an eigenvalue of A+E that is not an eigenvalue of A. Then 1≤‖(A−μI)−1E‖≤‖(A−μI)−1‖‖E‖.

lem-simple-eigenvalue-left-right.title: Left and Right Eigenvectors of a Simple Eigenvalue
lem-simple-eigenvalue-left-right.title_html: Left and Right Eigenvectors of a Simple Eigenvalue
lem-simple-eigenvalue-left-right.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and let λ be a simple eigenvalue of A, with a right eigenvector x and a left eigenvector y.

  1. The right eigenvectors of A for λ are exactly the non-zero multiples of x, and the left eigenvectors are exactly the non-zero multiples of y.
  2. y∗x≠0.

lem-sorted-pairing.title: The Sorted Pairing Is Cheapest
lem-sorted-pairing.html: Let a1≥a2≥⋯≥an and b1≥b2≥⋯≥bn be real numbers. Then for every σ∈Sn, ∑i=1n(ai−bi)2 ≤ ∑i=1n(ai−bσ(i))2.

lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit.title: Moving Factors in and out of the Two Norms
lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit.title_html: Moving Factors in and out of the Two Norms
lem-spectral-frobenius-toolkit.html:
Let ‖⋅‖ stand for either ‖⋅‖2 or ‖⋅‖F, the same one throughout each statement.

  1. ‖M∗‖=‖M‖ for every M∈Mm×n(C).
  2. ‖XMY‖≤‖X‖2‖M‖‖Y‖2 whenever the product is defined.
  3. If X∈Mm×k(C) has orthonormal columns, that is X∗X=Ik, then ‖X‖2=1, ‖XM‖=‖M‖ and ‖X∗N‖≤‖N‖ for all M∈Mk×n(C) and N∈Mm×n(C). In particular ‖UMV‖=‖M‖ for unitary U and V.

prp-eigenvalue-condition-properties.title: Properties of the Eigenvalue Condition Number
prp-eigenvalue-condition-properties.title_html: Properties of the Eigenvalue Condition Number
prp-eigenvalue-condition-properties.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) and let λ be a simple eigenvalue of A with right eigenvector x and left eigenvector y.

  1. κA(λ) does not depend on the choice of x and y, and κA(λ)≥1, with equality if and only if y is a multiple of x.
  2. For every E∈Mn(C), the eigenvalue λ(t) of @thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative satisfies |λ′(0)|≤κA(λ)‖E‖2. Equality holds for E=yx∗/(‖x‖‖y‖), which has ‖E‖2=1. Hence κA(λ)=max{|λ′(0)|:‖E‖2=1}.
  3. If A is normal, then κA(μ)=1 for every simple eigenvalue μ of A.
  4. If A=XΛX−1 with X invertible and Λ=diag(λ1,…,λn), and λi is simple, then κA(λi)≤κ2(X).
  5. κA(λ)=1/cos⁡θ, where θ∈[0,π/2) is the principal angle between the lines span(x) and span(y) (@def-principal-angles).

prp-gershgorin-scaling.title: Rescaling the Gershgorin Discs
prp-gershgorin-scaling.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), let d1,…,dn be positive real numbers, and D=diag(d1,…,dn). Then:

  1. D−1AD has entries aijdj/di. It has the same diagonal as A, and the same eigenvalues with the same algebraic multiplicities.
  2. ri(D−1AD)=1di∑j≠i|aij|dj for each i.
  3. Every eigenvalue of A lies in ⋃i=1n{z:|z−aii|≤1di∑j≠i|aij|dj}.

prp-numerical-range-basic.title: Basic Properties of the Numerical Range
prp-numerical-range-basic.title_html: Basic Properties of the Numerical Range
prp-numerical-range-basic.html:
Let A∈Mn(C).

  1. spec(A)⊆W(A).
  2. W(αA+βI)=αW(A)+β:={αw+β:w∈W(A)} for all α,β∈C.
  3. W(U∗AU)=W(A) for every unitary U∈Mn(C).
  4. W(A) is compact: every sequence in W(A) has a subsequence converging to a point of W(A). In particular W(A) is closed.
  5. W(A)⊆{z:|z|≤‖A‖2}.

prp-numerical-range-normal.title: The Numerical Range of a Normal Matrix
prp-numerical-range-normal.title_html: The Numerical Range of a Normal Matrix
prp-numerical-range-normal.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be normal, with eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, listed with multiplicity. Then W(A)=conv{λ1,…,λn}.

prp-principal-angles-well-defined.title: Principal Angles Are Well Defined
prp-principal-angles-well-defined.html:
In the setting of @def-principal-angles, put M=QW∗QU∈Ml×k(F).

  1. The singular values of M do not depend on the choice of the orthonormal basis matrices QU and QW.
  2. 1≥σ1(M)≥⋯≥σk(M)≥0, so θ1,…,θk exist, are unique, and are non-decreasing.
  3. σi(QU∗QW)=σi(M) for i=1,…,k. In particular, if k=l, the principal angles between W and U are those between U and W.
  4. If k=1 and U=span(u) with ‖u‖=1, then cos⁡θ1=‖PWu‖. If also l=1 and W=span(w) with ‖w‖=1, then cos⁡θ1=|⟨u,w⟩|.

prp-principal-vectors.title: Principal Vectors
prp-principal-vectors.html: In the setting of @def-principal-angles, let QW∗QU=YΣZ∗ be a singular value decomposition (@thm-svd), with Y∈Ml(F) and Z∈Mk(F) unitary, columns y1,…,yl and z1,…,zk. Put ui=QUzi (1≤i≤k),wj=QWyj (1≤j≤l). Then (u1,…,uk) is an orthonormal basis of U, (w1,…,wl) is an orthonormal basis of W, and ⟨ui,wj⟩={cos⁡θiif i=j,0if i≠j.

prp-sep-properties.title: Properties of the Separation
prp-sep-properties.html:
Let A∈Mm(C), B∈Mn(C), and K=In⊗A−B⊤⊗Im.

  1. The minimum defining sepF(A,B) exists, and sepF(A,B)=σmn(K), the smallest singular value of K.
  2. sepF(A,B)>0 if and only if spec(A)∩spec(B)=∅.
  3. sepF(A,B)≤mini,j|λi−μj|.
  4. If spec(A)∩spec(B)=∅, then for every C the unique solution of AX−XB=C satisfies ‖X‖F≤‖C‖FsepF(A,B), and equality holds for some C≠0.
  5. For unitary U∈U(m) and V∈U(n), sepF(U∗AU,V∗BV)=sepF(A,B).
  6. If n=1 and B=(μ), then sepF(A,B)=σm(A−μIm), the smallest singular value of A−μIm.

thm-bauer-fike.title: Bauer–Fike Theorem
thm-bauer-fike.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be diagonalizable. Write A=XΛX−1, where X is invertible and Λ is the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries λ1,…,λn. Let E∈Mn(C) be arbitrary, and let p∈{1,2,∞}. Then every eigenvalue μ of A+E satisfies min1≤i≤n|λi−μ|≤κp(X)‖E‖p.

thm-bauer-fike-defective.title: Bauer–Fike for a Jordan Form
thm-bauer-fike-defective.html: Let A=XJX−1∈Mn(C), where X is invertible and J is a Jordan form of A whose largest block has size m. Let λ1,…,λn be the eigenvalues of A, let E∈Mn(C), and put θ=mκ2(X)‖E‖2. Then every eigenvalue μ of A+E satisfies min1≤i≤n|λi−μ|≤max(θ,θ1/m).

thm-bendixson.title: Bendixson’s Theorem
thm-bendixson.html: Let A∈Mn(C), with H=(A+A∗)/2 and K=(A−A∗)/(2i). Every w∈W(A) satisfies λn(H)≤Rew≤λ1(H),λn(K)≤Imw≤λ1(K). In particular every eigenvalue λ of A satisfies the same inequalities with λ in place of w.

thm-brauer-ovals.title: Brauer’s Ovals of Cassini
thm-brauer-ovals.html:
Let n≥2 and A∈Mn(C). For i≠j put Oij(A):={z∈C:|z−aii||z−ajj|≤ri(A)rj(A)}.

  1. Every eigenvalue of A lies in ⋃i≠jOij(A).
  2. Oij(A)⊆Di(A)∪Dj(A) for every i≠j. Hence ⋃i≠jOij(A)⊆⋃iDi(A).

thm-davis-kahan-frobenius.title: The Davis–Kahan \sin\Theta Theorem
thm-davis-kahan-frobenius.title_html: The Davis–Kahan sin⁡Θ Theorem
thm-davis-kahan-frobenius.html: Let A,A~=A+E∈Mn(C) be Hermitian, let 1≤k≤n−1, and let Q=(Q1Q2) and Q~=(Q~1Q~2) be unitary, with Q1,Q~1∈Mn×k(C), such that Q∗AQ=Λ1⊕Λ2,Q~∗A~Q~=Λ~1⊕Λ~2 are real diagonal. Suppose there is a δ>0 such that |μ−λ|≥δ for every diagonal entry μ of Λ~2 and every diagonal entry λ of Λ1. Then the principal angles Θ=Θ(col(Q1),col(Q~1)) satisfy ‖sin⁡Θ‖F ≤ ‖EQ1‖Fδ ≤ k‖E‖2δ.

thm-davis-kahan-one-sided.title: The \sin\Theta Theorem, One-Sided Case
thm-davis-kahan-one-sided.title_html: The sin⁡Θ Theorem, One-Sided Case
thm-davis-kahan-one-sided.html:
In the setting of @thm-davis-kahan-frobenius, suppose instead that there are a∈R and δ>0 such that either

  1. every eigenvalue in Λ1 is ≥a and every eigenvalue in Λ~2 is ≤a−δ, or
  2. every eigenvalue in Λ1 is ≤a and every eigenvalue in Λ~2 is ≥a+δ.

Then ‖sin⁡Θ‖2=sin⁡θk ≤ ‖EQ1‖2δ ≤ ‖E‖2δ.

thm-elsner-matching.title: Elsner’s Matching Bound
thm-elsner-matching.html: Let A,B∈Mn(C) have eigenvalues λ1,…,λn and μ1,…,μn, and put R=(‖A‖2+‖B‖2)1−1/n‖A−B‖21/n. Then the μi can be numbered so that |λi−μi|≤(2n−1)R for every i.

thm-elsner-spectral-variation.title: Elsner’s Spectral Variation Bound
thm-elsner-spectral-variation.html: Let A,B∈Mn(C), and let λ1,…,λn be the eigenvalues of A. Then every eigenvalue μ of B satisfies min1≤i≤n|λi−μ|≤(‖A‖2+‖B‖2)1−1/n‖A−B‖21/n. (For n=1 the first factor is 1.)

thm-gershgorin.title: Gershgorin’s Theorem
thm-gershgorin.html:
Let n≥1, A∈Mn(C), and let λ be an eigenvalue of A with eigenvector x=(x1,…,xn). If k is an index with |xk|=maxj|xj|, then λ∈Dk(A). Consequently:

  1. every eigenvalue of A lies in the union D1(A)∪⋯∪Dn(A) of the row discs;
  2. every eigenvalue of A lies in the union D1(A⊤)∪⋯∪Dn(A⊤) of the column discs;
  3. hence every eigenvalue lies in the intersection of the two unions.

thm-gershgorin-counting.title: Gershgorin’s Counting Theorem
thm-gershgorin-counting.html: Let A∈Mn(C), let S⊆{1,…,n} have k elements with 1≤k≤n−1, and put U=⋃i∈SDi(A),V=⋃i∉SDi(A). If U∩V=∅, then U contains exactly k eigenvalues of A and V contains exactly n−k, counted with algebraic multiplicity.

thm-hermitian-residual-bound.title: Residual Bound for Hermitian Matrices
thm-hermitian-residual-bound.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian, let x∈Cn with ‖x‖=1, let μ∈R, and put r=Ax−μx. Then some eigenvalue λ of A satisfies |λ−μ|≤‖r‖; that is, the interval [μ−‖r‖,μ+‖r‖] contains an eigenvalue of A.

thm-hoffman-wielandt.title: Hoffman–Wielandt Theorem
thm-hoffman-wielandt.html: Let A,B∈Mn(C) be normal, with eigenvalues λ1,…,λn and μ1,…,μn respectively, each listed with algebraic multiplicity in any order. Then there is a permutation σ∈Sn with ∑i=1n|λi−μσ(i)|2 ≤ ‖A−B‖F2.

thm-kato-temple.title: Kato–Temple Theorem
thm-kato-temple.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian, let x∈Cn with ‖x‖=1, let μ=x∗Ax, and let ε=‖Ax−μx‖.

  1. Let β>μ, and let λ<β be an eigenvalue of A such that no eigenvalue of A lies in the open interval (λ,β). Then λ ≥ μ−ε2β−μ.
  2. Let α<μ, and let λ>α be an eigenvalue of A such that no eigenvalue of A lies in the open interval (α,λ). Then λ ≤ μ+ε2μ−α.

In particular, if α<μ<β and λ is the only eigenvalue of A in (α,β), then μ−ε2β−μ ≤ λ ≤ μ+ε2μ−α.

thm-mirsky-frobenius.title: Mirsky’s Theorem
thm-mirsky-frobenius.html: Let A,B∈Mm×n(C) and p=min(m,n). Then ∑i=1p(σi(A)−σi(B))2 ≤ ‖A−B‖F2.

thm-ostrowski-relative.title: Ostrowski’s Theorem
thm-ostrowski-relative.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian and let S∈Mn(C) be invertible. Then SS∗ is positive definite, and for each k=1,…,n there is a real number θk with λk(SAS∗)=θkλk(A),λn(SS∗) ≤ θk ≤ λ1(SS∗). In particular θk>0, and |λk(SAS∗)−λk(A)| ≤ ‖SS∗−I‖2|λk(A)|.

thm-polar-positive-perturbation.title: Perturbation of the Positive Polar Factor
thm-polar-positive-perturbation.title_html: Perturbation of the Positive Polar Factor
thm-polar-positive-perturbation.html: Let A,B∈Mn(C) be invertible. Then ‖|A|−|B|‖ ≤ (‖A‖2+‖B‖2)‖A−B‖σn(A)+σn(B), where ‖⋅‖ is either ‖⋅‖2 or ‖⋅‖F.

thm-polar-unitary-perturbation.title: Perturbation of the Unitary Polar Factor
thm-polar-unitary-perturbation.title_html: Perturbation of the Unitary Polar Factor
thm-polar-unitary-perturbation.html: Let A,B∈Mn(C) be invertible, with polar decompositions (@thm-polar-decomposition) A=UP and B=VQ, where U,V are unitary, P=|A| and Q=|B|. Then ‖U−V‖ ≤ 2‖A−B‖σn(A)+σn(B), where ‖⋅‖ is either ‖⋅‖2 or ‖⋅‖F.

thm-projection-difference-norm.title: The Distance Between Projections
thm-projection-difference-norm.html:
Let U,W⊆Fn with dim⁡U=dim⁡W=k≥1, and principal angles θ1≤⋯≤θk. Then

  1. ‖PU−PW‖2=sin⁡θk;
  2. ‖PU−PW‖F=2‖sin⁡Θ(U,W)‖F;
  3. ‖PU−PW‖2≤1, with equality if and only if U∩W⊥≠{0}.

thm-residual-bound.title: Residual Bound
thm-residual-bound.html: Let A=XΛX−1∈Mn(C) be diagonalizable, with Λ=diag(λ1,…,λn). Let μ∈C and x^∈Cn with x^≠0, and let η≥0 satisfy ‖Ax^−μx^‖2≤η‖x^‖2. Then some eigenvalue λi of A satisfies |λi−μ|≤κ2(X)η. If A is normal, some eigenvalue satisfies |λi−μ|≤η.

thm-roots-continuous.title: Continuous Dependence of the Roots on the Coefficients
thm-roots-continuous.title_html: Continuous Dependence of the Roots on the Coefficients
thm-roots-continuous.html: Let n≥1 and let p(x)=xn+cn−1xn−1+⋯+c1x+c0∈C[x] be monic, with roots μ1,…,μn∈C listed with multiplicity. Let ε>0. Then there is δ>0 with the following property. If q(x)=xn+bn−1xn−1+⋯+b1x+b0 is monic of the same degree n and |bj−cj|<δ for every j, then the roots ν1,…,νn of q, listed with multiplicity, can be numbered so that |νi−μi|<ε for i=1,…,n.

thm-sep-normal.title: Separation of Normal Matrices
thm-sep-normal.html: Let A∈Mm(C) and B∈Mn(C) be normal, with eigenvalues λ1,…,λm and μ1,…,μn. Then sepF(A,B)=mini,j|λi−μj|. Consequently, if δ=mini,j|λi−μj|>0, the unique solution of AX−XB=C satisfies ‖X‖F≤‖C‖F/δ.

thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative.title: Derivative of a Simple Eigenvalue
thm-simple-eigenvalue-derivative.html:
Let A∈Mn(C), let λ be a simple eigenvalue of A with a right eigenvector x and a left eigenvector y, and let E∈Mn(C). Then there are r>0 and t0>0 with the following properties.

  1. For every real t with |t|<t0, the matrix A+tE has exactly one eigenvalue, counted with algebraic multiplicity, in the open disc {z∈C:|z−λ|<r}. Call it λ(t). Thus λ(0)=λ, and λ(t) is a simple eigenvalue of A+tE.
  2. λ(t)→λ as t→0.
  3. The function t↦λ(t) is differentiable at t=0, and λ′(0)=limt→0λ(t)−λt=y∗Exy∗x.

thm-sines-of-principal-angles.title: Sines of Principal Angles
thm-sines-of-principal-angles.html:
Let U,W⊆Fn with 1≤k=dim⁡U≤l=dim⁡W, principal angles θ1≤⋯≤θk, and orthonormal basis matrices QU,QW.

  1. Suppose l<n, and let QW⊥∈Mn×(n−l)(F) be an orthonormal basis matrix of W⊥. Put M=QW∗QU and N=QW⊥∗QU∈M(n−l)×k(F). Then M∗M+N∗N=Ik, and the eigenvalues of N∗N, with multiplicity, are sin2⁡θ1,…,sin2⁡θk. Equivalently, σi(N)=sin⁡θk+1−i for i=1,…,k, with the convention for σi stated at the start of the section.
  2. For every l≤n, ‖(I−PW)PU‖2=‖(I−PW)QU‖2=sin⁡θk=‖sin⁡Θ(U,W)‖2, and ‖(I−PW)PU‖F=‖(I−PW)QU‖F=‖sin⁡Θ(U,W)‖F.

thm-sqrt-perturbation.title: Perturbation of the Square Root
thm-sqrt-perturbation.html: Let P,Q∈Mn(C) be positive definite. Then ‖P1/2−Q1/2‖ ≤ ‖P−Q‖λn(P)1/2+λn(Q)1/2, where ‖⋅‖ is either ‖⋅‖2 or ‖⋅‖F.

thm-sylvester-one-sided.title: One-Sided Sylvester Bound
thm-sylvester-one-sided.html: Let A∈Mm(C) and B∈Mn(C) be Hermitian, and let α>β be real numbers with A⪰αIm,B⪯βIn. Then for every C∈Mm×n(C) the equation AX−XB=C has exactly one solution, and it satisfies ‖X‖2≤‖C‖2α−β,‖X‖F≤‖C‖Fα−β.

thm-taussky.title: Taussky’s Theorem
thm-taussky.html: Let n≥1, let A∈Mn(C) be irreducible, and let λ be an eigenvalue of A with |λ−aii|≥ri(A)for **every** i, that is, λ lies in no open disc {|z−aii|<ri(A)}. Then |λ−aii|=ri(A) for every i: the eigenvalue lies on the boundary circle of every Gershgorin disc. Moreover, every eigenvector for λ has all its coordinates of the same modulus. The hypothesis holds in particular when λ is a boundary point (@def-interior-point) of D1(A)∪⋯∪Dn(A).

thm-toeplitz-hausdorff.title: Toeplitz–Hausdorff Theorem
thm-toeplitz-hausdorff.html: For every A∈Mn(C), the numerical range W(A) is a convex subset of C.
